question.text: A red solid is insoluble in water. However, it becomes soluble if some  <math><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></math>  is added to water. Heating the red solid in a test tube results in liberation of some violet coloured fumes and droplets of a metal appear on the cooler parts of the test tube. The red solid is

solution.text: <math><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>  is orange-red in appearance and hardly soluble in water. It dissolves in excess of  <math><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo></mrow></msup></math>   giving complexes  <math><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>  and  <math><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>-</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> . Violet fumes are liberated due to the release of Iodine gas upon heating.
